title: Open Arms
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2008, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 2008 · constellation Pictor · about 450 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #98 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: The spiral galaxy NGC 2008 takes center stage in this Hubble image, its ghostly arms spreading out toward us. It lies roughly 425 million light-years away in the constellation Pictor, the Painter's Easel.

Discovered by John Herschel in 1834, NGC 2008 is classed as type Sc in the Hubble sequence, a system for sorting galaxies by shape. The S marks it as a spiral, and the c means it has a fairly small central bulge and more open arms. Spirals with bigger bulges tend to have more tightly wound arms and are classed Sa, with type Sb in between.

Spirals are everywhere, making up over 70% of all observed galaxies, the Milky Way among them. Being common doesn't make them any less beautiful. These huge, whirling collections of billions of stars rank among the most memorable sights that telescopes like Hubble have recorded.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.61 x 1.57 arcminutes) and distance (450 million light years), the frame spans roughly 342,000 × 206,000 light-years. Its light set out about 450 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed in visible and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye.
